pergunta: Include at least 10 single-word palindromes, each at least 5 characters long. Prove that a step function f / [a, b] -> \mathbb{R} is Riemann Integrable.
resposta:
**Palindromes (single‑word, ≥ 5 letters)**  
level radar civic refer madam rotor kayak solos stats tenet  

---

### Proof that a step function \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}\) is Riemann integrable  

A **step function** on \([a,b]\) is a bounded function for which there exists a finite partition  

\[
a=x_{0}<x_{1}<\dots <x_{n}=b
\]

such that \(f\) is constant on each sub‑interval \([x_{i-1},x_{i}]\) (the values at the partition points themselves do not affect the integral).  
Denote the constant value on \([x_{i-1},x_{i}]\) by \(c_{i}\in\mathbb{R}\).

---

#### 1. Upper and lower sums coincide  

For any sub‑interval \(I_i=[x_{i-1},x_i]\) we have  

\[
\sup_{x\in I_i} f(x)=\inf_{x\in I_i} f(x)=c_i .
\]

Hence the **upper Darboux sum** and the **lower Darboux sum** for the partition \(P=\{x_0,\dots ,x_n\}\) are  

\[
U(P,f)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i\,(x_i-x_{i-1}),\qquad 
L(P,f)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i\,(x_i-x_{i-1}).
\]

Therefore  

\[
U(P,f)-L(P,f)=0 .
\]

---

#### 2. Riemann’s criterion  

A bounded function on a closed interval is Riemann integrable iff for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists a partition \(P\) with \(U(P,f)-L(P,f)<\varepsilon\).  
Since we have found a partition (in fact any partition that contains the jump points) for which the difference is **exactly zero**, the condition holds for every \(\varepsilon>0\). Consequently \(f\) is Riemann integrable on \([a,b]\).

---

#### 3. Value of the integral  

When the above partition is used, the common value of the upper and lower sums gives the integral:

\[
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i\,(x_i-x_{i-1}).
\]

---

#### 4. Alternative viewpoint (Lebesgue’s criterion)  

Step functions have only finitely many points of discontinuity (the endpoints of the sub‑intervals). A bounded function whose set of discontinuities has Lebesgue measure zero is Riemann integrable. Since a finite set has measure zero, the result follows immediately.

---

Thus every step function \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfies the definition of Riemann integrability, and its integral is given by the sum of the constant pieces multiplied by their lengths.

A paper about text-to-image AIs defines "zero-shot generalization" as "the ability of the model to apply its learned knowledge to new unseen concepts," citing a 2013 paper. Is this a sensible definition for text-to-image AIs?
resposta:
Emma, Liam, and Sophia would likely agree that the definition given in the paper is on the right track for describing zero‑shot generalization in text‑to‑image AI systems.  

The phrase “the ability of the model to apply its learned knowledge to new unseen concepts” captures the core idea that a zero‑shot model should be able to take a prompt it has never seen during training and still produce a coherent image. In other words, the model must extrapolate from the visual knowledge it has acquired (e.g., patterns of shapes, colors, objects) to novel textual descriptions such as “a futuristic city made of crystal” when the training data only contained more conventional scenes.  

That said, the definition is a bit narrow for the specific challenges of text‑to‑image generation. Zero‑shot performance in this domain also depends on the model’s capacity for **compositional reasoning** (mixing multiple objects or attributes), **style transfer**, and handling of **rare or abstract visual concepts** that were never represented in the training set. Prove that the product of two primitive polynomials in a UFD \(R[x]\) is primitive, and that coprimality in \(R[x]\) lifts to coprimality in the fraction field \(F[x]\).

---

### 1. Primitive polynomials and Gauss’s Lemma  

Recall that a polynomial \(h(x)=a_nx^n+\dots +a_0\in R[x]\) is **primitive** if the greatest common divisor of its coefficients in the UFD \(R\) is a unit; equivalently, the **content** \(c_R(h)=\gcd(a_0,\dots ,a_n)\) satisfies \(c_R(h)\in R^\times\).

Let \(f,g\in R[x]\) be primitive. Assume, for a contradiction, that the product \(fg\) is not primitive. Then there exists a prime element \(\pi\in R\) that divides every coefficient of \(fg\). Reduce the coefficients modulo \(\pi\): denote by \(\overline{h}\) the image of \(h\) in \((R/(\pi))[x]\). Since \(\pi\) is prime, \(R/(\pi)\) is an integral domain, and therefore \((R/(\pi))[x]\) is also an integral domain.

From \(fg\) having all coefficients divisible by \(\pi\) we obtain  
\[
\overline{f}\,\overline{g}=0\quad\text{in }(R/(\pi))[x].
\]
Because \((R/(\pi))[x]\) has no zero‑divisors, either \(\overline{f}=0\) or \(\overline{g}=0\). The former means that every coefficient of \(f\) is a multiple of \(\pi\), contradicting the primitivity of \(f\); the latter contradicts the primitivity of \(g\). Hence no such \(\pi\) exists, and \(fg\) is primitive. This is the classical Gauss’s Lemma for polynomials over a UFD.

---

### 2. Coprimality in \(R[x]\) versus \(F[x]\)

Let \(f,g\in R[x]\) be **coprime** in \(R[x]\); by definition there exist \(a,b\in R[x]\) such that  
\[
af+bg=1\qquad\text{(Bezout identity)}.
\tag{1}
\]

Since the inclusion \(R[x]\hookrightarrow F[x]\) (where \(F=\operatorname{Frac}(R)\)) is a ring homomorphism, identity (1) remains valid in \(F[x]\). Consequently the ideal generated by \(f\) and \(g\) in \(F[x]\) contains the unit \(1\); i.e. \((f,g)=F[x]\). Thus \(f\) and \(g\) are coprime in \(F[x]\).

For completeness, we argue directly: suppose a non‑constant \(h\in F[x]\) divided both \(f\) and \(g\) in \(F[x]\). Write \(h=p/q\) with \(p,q\in R[x]\) and \(\gcd(p,q)=1\). From \(f=h\,u\) and \(g=h\,v\) with \(u,v\in F[x]\) we obtain after clearing denominators a non‑zero \(c\in R\) such that \(c u,\,c v\in R[x]\) and  
\[
c f=(c h)u,\qquad c g=(c h)v .
\]
Hence \(c h\) is a common divisor of \(c f\) and \(c g\) in \(R[x]\). Since \(c\) is a unit in the field \(F\), \(c h\) is associate to \(h\) in \(F[x]\). If \(h\) were non‑constant, \(c h\) would be a non‑unit common divisor of \(f\) and \(g\) in \(R[x]\), contradicting the hypothesis that they are coprime. Therefore \(h\) must be a unit of \(F[x]\), i.e. a non‑zero constant, and \(f,g\) are coprime in \(F[x]\).

---

Both statements are established: the product of primitive polynomials in a UFD remains primitive, and coprimality in the polynomial ring over a UFD carries over to its field of fractions. ∎

resposta:
In this exposition we maintain a **level** view, **radar** emphasis, **civic** rigor, **refer** insight, **rotor** stability, **kayak** rhythm, **solos** clarity, **stats** verification, **tenet** logic, **madam** harmony. The goal is to show that for odd primes \(p>3\) the polynomial \(f(x)=x^{2}+3x+3\) possesses a root modulo \(p\) precisely when \(p\equiv1\pmod{3}\).

---

### Proof  

For a quadratic \(ax^{2}+bx+c\) over \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\) a root exists iff its discriminant \(D=b^{2}-4ac\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(p\).  
Here  

\[
D = 3^{2}-4\cdot1\cdot3 = 9-12 = -3 .
\]

Hence \(f(x)\) has a root in \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\) exactly when the Legendre symbol  

\[
\left(\frac{-3}{p}\right)=1 .
\]

Using the multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol and quadratic reciprocity,

\[
\left(\frac{-3}{p}\right)=\left(\frac{-1}{p}\right)\left(\frac{3}{p}\right).
\]

We know  

\[
\left(\frac{-1}{p}\right)=(-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}},\qquad 
\left(\frac{3}{p}\right)=\left(\frac{p}{3}\right)(-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}}
\]

because \((3-1)/2=1\). Multiplying these expressions, the factors \((-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\) cancel, giving  

\[
\left(\frac{-3}{p}\right)=\left(\frac{p}{3}\right).
\]

Since \(3\) is prime, \(\left(\frac{p}{3}\right)=1\) precisely when \(p\equiv1\pmod{3}\), and \(\left(\frac{p}{3}\right)=-1\) when \(p\equiv2\pmod{3}\). Consequently  

\[
\left(\frac{-3}{p}\right)=1 \iff p\equiv1\pmod{3}.
\]

Thus the quadratic \(x^{2}+3x+3\) has a root modulo an odd prime \(p>3\) **if and only if** \(p\equiv1\pmod{3}\). ∎

Even though Majid is usually portrayed as a cunning, indifferent figure, the excerpt from **Part Four (p. 153)** shows him stepping out of the house carrying Jamila wrapped in a thin quilt while a bewildered Rahima trails behind him, the brilliant moonlight initially blinding him. The act of physically shielding the vulnerable suggests a protective impulse that goes beyond his typical self‑serving scheming. In this brief moment his demeanor shifts from detached calculation to a visible willingness to rescue, hinting that his motive may be rooted in a sense of duty rather than pure self‑interest.

If we read his motive through a **deontological** lens, the rescue would be seen as an adherence to a moral rule—“help those in peril”—independent of the consequences. The scene itself presents the rescue as a right thing to do, irrespective of how it serves Majid’s own goals. Conversely, a **teleological** reading would emphasize the strategic calculation behind the act: the darkness, the moon’s glare, and the need for swift movement all serve a calculated end, protecting the two women from further danger. The fact that he initiates the plan under the cover of night and uses the moon’s light only as a temporary obstacle points to a well‑planned, outcome‑oriented motive.

Thus, while the passage still retains traces of Majid’s cunning (he chooses the optimal moment to act) and his usual apathy (the rescue is still framed as a personal mission), the dominant impression is that he is acting out of a **calculated benevolence**—a blend of strategic foresight and an emergent sense of responsibility. Whether one labels it deontological or teleological depends on whether the focus is on the moral rule he follows or the practical result he secures.
